scope: Prove degree-one invariance directly for smooth modifications, use a common graph resolution for Lee--Gauduchon invariance, and deduce the span assertion from openness.

edits.old: Gauduchon's theorem makes $\mathcal Z_X^+$ nonempty. It is convex and stable under positive scaling. Fix $\Gamma_0\in\mathcal Z_X^+$. For every $\Gamma\in\mathcal Z_X$, compactness implies $\Gamma+t\Gamma_0>0$ for large $t$. Thus $\mathcal Z_X^+$ spans $\mathcal Z_X$, proving the span assertion.
edits.new: Gauduchon's theorem makes $\mathcal Z_X^+$ nonempty. It is convex and stable under positive scaling.

edits.old: To see openness directly, choose forms $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_r\in\mathcal Z_X$ whose images form a basis of $W_X$. If $\Gamma\in\mathcal Z_X^+$, then $\Gamma+\sum_i t_i\Gamma_i$ remains strictly positive for all sufficiently small real $t_i$. Its image describes a neighborhood of $q_X(\Gamma)$ in $W_X$. This also covers $W_X=\{0\}$, with the empty basis.
edits.new: To see openness directly, choose forms $\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_r\in\mathcal Z_X$ whose images form a basis of $W_X$. If $\Gamma\in\mathcal Z_X^+$, then $\Gamma+\sum_i t_i\Gamma_i$ remains strictly positive for all sufficiently small real $t_i$. Its image describes a neighborhood of $q_X(\Gamma)$ in $W_X$. This also covers $W_X=\{0\}$, with the empty basis. Since a nonempty open subset spans its ambient vector space, the span assertion follows.

edits.old:
A blowup along a divisor is an isomorphism. Otherwise let $Z$ be the center, of complex codimension $r\geq2$, and $E$ the exceptional divisor. Identify
$U=X\setminus Z=Y\setminus E$. By the Thom isomorphism and the long exact sequence of the pair,
\[
 H^k(X,U;\R)=H^{k-2r}(Z;\R)=0\quad(k=1,2).
\]
Hence restriction $H^1(X,\R)\to H^1(U,\R)$ is an isomorphism. On $Y$, the same argument gives $H^1(Y,U;\R)=H^{-1}(E;\R)=0$, so restriction $H^1(Y,\R)\to H^1(U,\R)$ is injective. It is also surjective: every class on $U$ extends to $X$, and its pullback extends it to $Y$. Commutativity of restrictions proves the first assertion. For a disconnected center the argument applies to each disjoint component. Poincar\'e duality and the projection formula give the second assertion.
edits.new:
For a proper analytic subset $A$ of a connected complex manifold $M$, restriction
$H^1(M,\R)\to H^1(M\setminus A,\R)$ is injective, and is an isomorphism
if $A$ has complex codimension at least two. Indeed, choose a Whitney
stratification of $A$. General position moves every one-cycle off its
strata, which have real codimension at least two. If those codimensions
are at least four, it also moves every bounding two-chain off the strata,
relative to its boundary. Thus the map on first homology is surjective
in the first case and bijective in the second. Dualizing over $\R$ gives
the asserted restriction statements.

Since $X$ is smooth, there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of complex
codimension at least two such that $\pi$ is an isomorphism over
$U=X\setminus A$. Restriction from $X$ to $U$ is therefore an isomorphism,
whereas restriction from $Y$ to $\pi^{-1}U$ is injective. Every class on
$\pi^{-1}U\simeq U$ extends to $X$ and hence pulls back to a class on $Y$.
The commutative restriction diagram proves that $\pi^*$ is an isomorphism.
Poincar\'e duality and the projection formula give the assertion for $\pi_*$.

edits.old: For a general bimeromorphic map, use the standard analytic weak factorization theorem: it factors into blowups and blowdowns along smooth centers between compact complex manifolds \cite[Theorem 0.3.1, analytic case]{AKMW02}. Apply the preceding argument at every step. These degree-one identifications are the natural ones and do not depend on the chosen factorization. Indeed, they agree on a common open set where the bimeromorphic map is an isomorphism, and restriction to such a set is injective in degree one: one-dimensional cycles can be moved off the strata of its analytic complement, each of real codimension at least two. The dual identifications are consequently canonical as well.
edits.new:
For a bimeromorphic map between $X$ and $Y$, resolve its graph to obtain
modifications $p:Z\to X$ and $q:Z\to Y$ from one smooth compact manifold.
The preceding argument applies to both maps and identifies the cones and
kernels via $(q^*)^{-1}p^*$ and its Poincar\'e dual. These identifications
are independent of the resolution: they agree on a common open set where
the original map is an isomorphism, and the injectivity of degree-one
restriction proved above determines each class uniquely. The dual
identifications are consequently canonical as well.
